chunks: "An ADC turns an analog voltage into a number. Conceptually it does three things.
First it samples: at a fixed rate it grabs the input voltage and holds it steady, usually on a small capacitor, so the signal can't move while it's being measured.
Second it quantizes: it compares that held voltage against a reference and decides which of 2 to the N equal-sized bins it falls in.
Third it encodes that bin as an N-bit binary code. The relationship is code equals V in over V ref times 2 to the N . So a 12-bit ADC with a 3.
3 volts reference has 4096 codes and each LSB is about 0. 8 millivolts, and the inherent quantization error is up to half an LSB. How it finds the bin depends on the architecture.
A flash ADC uses one comparator per level, so it's very fast but needs 2 to the N-1 comparators.
A SAR ADC, which is what's inside most microcontrollers, does a binary search with one comparator and a DAC, taking N steps.
Delta-sigma ADCs oversample and filter to get very high resolution at low speed, which is what you'd see in a precision scale or audio codec.

The things I'd always watch are the reference, because it sets the scale, a low-pass filter ahead of the ADC so out-of-band noise doesn't alias, and the source impedance, because the sampling capacitor has to charge through it."
